“Ah! this is an antithesis!” he thought; and, throughout the good quarter of an hour that the scene Mathilde was making him still lasted, he thought of nothing but Madame de Rênal. In spite of himself, and although he often answered what Mathilde was saying to him, he could not tear his soul away from the memory of the bedroom at Verrières. He saw the Besançon Gazette upon the orange taffeta counterpane. He saw that very white hand clutching it convulsively; he saw Madame de Rênal weeping... He followed the path of every tear across that charming face.

Mademoiselle de La Mole, unable to obtain anything from Julien, had the lawyer brought in. Fortunately, he was a former captain in the Army of Italy of 1796, where he had been a comrade of Manuel’s.

For form’s sake, he opposed the condemned man’s decision. Wishing to treat him with esteem, Julien set out all his reasons for him.

“Upon my word, one may think as you do,” Monsieur Félix Vaneau—that was the lawyer’s name—finally told him. “But you have three full days in which to appeal, and it is my duty to return every day. If a volcano were to open beneath the prison, you would be saved within the next two months. You may die of illness,” he said, looking at Julien.

Julien shook his hand.

“I thank you; you are a fine man. I shall think about that.”

And when Mathilde finally left with the lawyer, he felt far more friendship for the lawyer than for her.




CHAPTER XLIII


An hour later, while he was sleeping soundly, he was awakened by tears that he felt running over his hand. “Ah! it is Mathilde again,” he thought, half awake. “Faithful to her theory, she has come to assail my resolve with tender feelings.” Wearied by the prospect of this new scene in the pathetic manner, he did not open his eyes. The verses about Belphégor fleeing his wife came back to his mind.

He heard a strange sigh; he opened his eyes: it was Madame de Rênal.

“Ah! I see you again before I die—is this an illusion?” he cried, throwing himself at her feet.

“But forgive me, madame; in your eyes I am nothing but a murderer,” he said at once, coming to his senses.

“Monsieur... I have come to implore you to appeal; I know that you do not wish to...” Her sobs choked her; she could not speak.

“Deign to forgive me.”

“If you want me to forgive you,” she told him, rising and throwing herself into his arms, “appeal your death sentence at once.”

Julien covered her with kisses.

“Will you come to see me every day during these two months?”

“I swear it to you. Every day, unless my husband forbids me.”

“I shall sign!” cried Julien. “What! You forgive me! Is it possible!”

He clasped her in his arms; he was beside himself. She gave a little cry.

“It is nothing,” she told him. “You hurt me.”

“On your shoulder!” cried Julien, bursting into tears. He drew back a little and covered her hand with fiery kisses. “Who could have told me, the last time I saw you, in your room at Verrières?...”

“Who could have told me then that I would write that infamous letter to Monsieur de La Mole?...”

“Know that I have always loved you, that I have loved no one but you.”

“Can it truly be possible!” cried Madame de Rênal, enraptured in her turn.

She leaned upon Julien, who was on his knees, and for a long time they wept in silence.

At no time in his life had Julien ever experienced such a moment.

A long while later, when they were able to speak:

“And that young Madame Michelet,” said Madame de Rênal, “or rather that Mademoiselle de La Mole, for I am truly beginning to believe this strange tale.”

“It is true only in appearance,” replied Julien. “She is my wife, but she is not my mistress...”

Interrupting each other a hundred times, they managed only with great difficulty to tell each other what they did not know. The letter written to Monsieur de La Mole had been composed by the young priest who guided Madame de Rênal’s conscience, and then copied out by her.

“What a horror religion made me commit!” she told him. “And even then I softened the most dreadful passages of that letter...”

Julien’s transports and happiness proved to her how completely he forgave her. Never had he been so madly in love.

“And yet I believe myself devout,” Madame de Rênal told him later in the conversation. “I sincerely believe in God; I also believe—and indeed it has been proven to me—that the crime I am committing is dreadful; and as soon as I see you, even after you fired two pistol shots at me...”

And here, despite her, Julien covered her with kisses.

“Let me be,” she continued. “I want to reason with you, for fear of forgetting it... As soon as I see you, all duties vanish; I am nothing but love for you—or rather, the word love is too weak. I feel for you what I ought to feel for God alone: a mingling of respect, love, obedience... In truth, I do not know what you inspire in me. If you told me to stab the jailer, the crime would be committed before I had thought about it. Explain this to me very clearly before I leave you; I want to see clearly into my heart, for in two months we shall part... By the way, shall we part?” she asked him with a smile.

“I take back my word!” cried Julien, rising. “I shall not appeal my death sentence if, by poison, knife, pistol, charcoal, or in any other manner whatsoever, you seek to put an end or an obstacle to your life.”

Madame de Rênal’s expression suddenly changed; the most intense tenderness gave way to profound reverie.

“What if we died at once?” she finally said to him.

“Who knows what one finds in the next life?” replied Julien. “Torments, perhaps; perhaps nothing at all. Can we not spend two months together in a delightful manner? Two months is a great many days. Never shall I have been so happy.”

“Never shall you have been so happy!”

“Never,” repeated Julien, enraptured, “and I am speaking to you as I speak to myself. God preserve me from exaggerating.”

“To speak in that way is to command me,” she said with a timid and melancholy smile.

“Well then! Swear, by the love you have for me, that you will not make any attempt upon your life by any direct or indirect means... Remember,” he added, “that you must live for my son, whom Mathilde will abandon to lackeys as soon as she is the Marquise de Croisenois.”
